tasks.title: Two Lines Between A and B: Cubic Speed and a Distance Table
tasks.context:
Elisabeth commutes regularly by train between stops $A$ and $B$. Line L1 is described by the velocity (in m/s)

$$v(t)=0.00002t^{3}-0.005t^{2}+0.4t$$

Line L1 passes through stop $B$ but does not stop there. Line L2 records the total travel distance from $A$ every $10$ seconds (table below). The run of L2 from $A$ to $B$ lasts $120$ seconds. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The minimal acceleration of Line L1 between stops $A$ and $B$ is reached before $t=75$.
The average velocity between the two stops $A$ and $B$ of Line L2 is more than $45$ km/h.
The velocity of Line L2 has only one local maximum.
The highest average velocity of Line L2 was reached between $60$ and $70$ seconds.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Deceleration means that the acceleration $a=v'$ is negative at that instant, so differentiate the cubic speed.

$$v(t)=0.00002t^{3}-0.005t^{2}+0.4t$$

$$a(t)=v'(t)=0.00006t^{2}-0.01t+0.4$$

Substitute $t=80$.

$$a(80)=0.00006\cdot 80^{2}-0.01\cdot 80+0.4=-0.016$$

The value is negative, so L1 is slowing down at $t=80$, so the statement is True.

**B.** → False

The acceleration of a cubic speed is a quadratic, so its minimum on the line occurs where $a'(t)=0$ and the leading coefficient of $a$ is positive.

$$a'(t)=0.00012t-0.01$$

$$0.00012t-0.01=0\implies t=\frac{0.01}{0.00012}=\frac{250}{3}$$

$$t=\frac{250}{3}\approx 83.3$$

That critical time is after $75$, not before it.

The minimal acceleration is reached near $t=83$, later than $t=75$, so the statement is False.

**C.** → False

A table gives interval averages as first differences over each time block, and a whole-run average as last distance over last time; converting metres per second into kilometres per hour uses the factor $3.6$.

$$v(t)=0.00002t^{3}-0.005t^{2}+0.4t$$

The whole-trip average speed of L2 is the last distance divided by the last time, then converted from m/s into km/h.

$$\bar v=\frac{1400}{120}=\frac{35}{3}\ \mathrm{m/s}$$

$$\frac{35}{3}\cdot 3.6=42\ \mathrm{km/h}$$

$42$ is not greater than $45$

That is not what the claim asserts, so the statement is False.

**D.** → False

On a discrete table the interval velocities are the first differences of distance over each $10$ s block.

$$\Delta s/\Delta t:\ 7,9,13,14,15,15,13,15,15,12,7,5$$

A local maximum of this sequence is a value strictly larger than both neighbours (or a plateau that falls on both sides). The plateau $15,15$ around $40$–$60$ s and the later plateau $15,15$ around $70$–$90$ s are two separate local peaks, with $13$ sitting between them.

There are two local maxima, not only one, so the statement is False.

**E.** → False

A table gives interval averages as first differences over each time block, and a whole-run average as last distance over last time; converting metres per second into kilometres per hour uses the factor $3.6$.

$$v(t)=0.00002t^{3}-0.005t^{2}+0.4t$$

The average velocity on $[60,70]$ is the corresponding first difference.

$$\frac{860-730}{10}=13\ \mathrm{m/s}$$

Several other blocks reach $15$ m/s, which is larger.

$$\frac{580-430}{10}=15\qquad \frac{1010-860}{10}=15$$

The highest interval average is $15$ m/s, not the $13$ on $[60,70]$

That is not what the claim asserts, so the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview: Differentiate the cubic speed of L1 to read acceleration; the second derivative locates the extreme of $a(t)$. For L2 the table gives interval average speeds as first differences over $10$ s, and the whole-trip average is total distance over $120$ s, converted by the factor $3.6$ from m/s into km/h.

tasks.title: Roots from a Factored Cubic
tasks.context: Let $p(x)=(x-1)(x+2)(x-3)$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.

A real root is where the graph meets the axis; factor first, then read the zeros from the linear factors.

$$p(x)=x^{3} - 2 x^{2} - 5 x + 6$$

$$x=1,\quad x=-2,\quad x=3$$

A real root is an input where the graph meets the horizontal axis, and a linear factor $x-a$ is present precisely when that happens at $x=a$. Meetings of two graphs are the roots of their difference. A product is zero precisely when one of the factors is zero. Those are the three roots.

tasks.title: A Line Times a Square
tasks.context: Let $p(x)=(2x-1)(x^{2}+1)$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The highest power of $x$ in $p$ is $x^{3}$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Work from the polynomial named in the stem: expand or factor as needed, then carry out the comparison the claim asks for.

$$p(x)=2 x^{3} - x^{2} + 2 x - 1$$

$$p(x)=2x^{3}-x^{2}+2x-1$$

The highest power and the number in front of it are read from the written rule: only a non-zero coefficient counts, and only the largest exponent that survives is the one that matters. The $x$ from the line times $x^{2}$ produces $x^{3}$. The highest power is $x^{3}$

That is the comparison the claim asked for, so the statement is True.

**B.** → True

A real root is where the graph meets the axis; factor first, then read the zeros from the linear factors.

$$p(x)=2 x^{3} - x^{2} + 2 x - 1$$

$$2x-1=0\implies x=\frac{1}{2}$$

A real root is an input where the graph meets the horizontal axis, and a linear factor $x-a$ is present precisely when that happens at $x=a$. Meetings of two graphs are the roots of their difference. $x^{2}+1$ never vanishes on $\mathbb{R}$, so the only real root comes from the line. That is the only real root.

That is the comparison the claim asked for, so the statement is True.

**C.** → True

Work from the polynomial named in the stem: expand or factor as needed, then carry out the comparison the claim asks for.

$$p(x)=2 x^{3} - x^{2} + 2 x - 1$$

$$p\left(0\right)=-1$$

A polynomial is evaluated by substituting the named input for every $x$ and simplifying the powers; the leftover number is the height of the graph there. Substituting $x=0$ into the written rule produces a single number, with no extra identity required. The value is $-1$, exactly the number named in the claim, so the statement is True.

**D.** → False

Work from the polynomial named in the stem: expand or factor as needed, then carry out the comparison the claim asks for.

$$p(x)=2 x^{3} - x^{2} + 2 x - 1$$

$$2x\cdot x^{2}=2x^{3}$$

The highest power and the number in front of it are read from the written rule: only a non-zero coefficient counts, and only the largest exponent that survives is the one that matters. The leading coefficient is $2$

The arithmetic does not match the claim, so the statement is False.

**E.** → False

Evenness and oddness are identities, not a glance at a single power: compare $p(-x)$ with $\pm p(x)$.

$$p(x)=2 x^{3} - x^{2} + 2 x - 1$$

$$p(-x)=- 2 x^{3} - x^{2} - 2 x - 1$$

Every even power survives the substitution $x\mapsto -x$ unchanged, while every odd power picks up a minus sign. That is the whole test: no extra coefficient arithmetic is required once the two sides have been written out.

$p(-x)$ is not $p(x)$, so the function is not even, so the statement is False.
